title: RAG: retrieval-augmented generation
subtitle: Ground answers in your own documents, check who may read them, and measure retrieval before you blame the model.

c.v: In November 2022, Jake Moffatt's grandmother died. The same day, Moffatt went to Air Canada's website to book a flight at its lower bereavement fares. Moffatt asked the website's support chatbot about these fares.

The chatbot said a passenger who had already travelled could ask for a reduced bereavement rate within 90 days of the ticket date. The words "bereavement fares" in its answer linked to the airline's own policy page. That page said the policy does not apply to requests made after travel is completed.

Moffatt trusted the chatbot, booked two flights, and applied for the lower rate within the 90 days. Air Canada staff then said the airline did not allow requests after travel. In an email, an airline representative admitted the chatbot had used "misleading words".

At the tribunal, Air Canada argued that it could not be held liable for what its chatbot said. The tribunal said this treats the chatbot as a separate legal entity, and called it "a remarkable submission". It said the airline is responsible for all the information on its website, whether it comes from a static page or a chatbot. It also asked why a customer should have to double-check one part of a website against another. The airline had to pay $812.02: $650.88 in damages, plus interest and tribunal fees.
Air Canada gave no information about how its chatbot worked, and the decision does not say how it was built.

But the lesson for anyone who ships one is clear. The answer and the policy page disagreed. Our advice: your system must answer from the real policy text, and show the user where the answer came from.
A language model alone is not enough for questions about
your
data. There are three reasons.
It has a
knowledge cutoff
Every model has a date after which its knowledge is not reliable. Anthropic lists this date for each Claude model.
Your price change from last week is not in it.
It has never seen your private data.
Your policies, tickets and contracts were not in its training data.
It can
hallucinate
Models sometimes write text that is false, or that does not match the text you gave them.
The
RAG
paper of 2020 described the core problem. When knowledge is stored only in model weights, it is hard to update, and hard to show where a fact came from.
Its answer was to add a second memory: a vector index of Wikipedia that the model reads from at answer time.
So RAG works like an open-book exam. Your app searches your documents, puts the few passages that matter in the prompt, and the model answers from them with citations.
The key idea.

In RAG, the model can only be as good as the text you give it. When an answer is wrong, first check whether retrieval found the right text. So treat retrieval as the main part of the system, and measure it.
Step through one request with Next and Back.
Before any question: index your documents
Chunk.
Split each document into small pieces. Anthropic says chunks are usually no more than a few hundred tokens.
Embed.
An
embedding model
turns each chunk into a vector, a list of numbers. The distance between two vectors measures how related the texts are.
Store.
Save each vector with its text, its source link, and who may read it. A
vector database
does this. So does Postgres with pgvector, which supports exact and approximate nearest-neighbour search.
At question time
Retrieve.
Embed the question the same way, and find the top k chunks with the nearest vectors. For how search indexes work in general, see
Search systems and inverted indexes
Filter.
Drop every chunk the user may not read.
Prompt.

Put the allowed chunks into the prompt, each with a number. Tell the model to use only these sources and to cite them. Let it say "I don't know" when the sources do not answer. Anthropic's guide lists all three methods to reduce hallucinations.
Answer.
Show the answer with links to the cited chunks, so the user can check.
Hybrid search and re-ranking
Vector search finds text with a similar
meaning
. But embeddings can miss exact matches, such as an error code like "TS-999".
BM25
is a keyword ranking function that finds exact words and phrases.
Hybrid search
runs both and merges the two lists.
One way to merge them is
reciprocal rank fusion
(RRF). Each result gets 1 / (k + rank) from each list, and the points are added up. Elasticsearch uses k = 60 by default.
RRF needs no tuning, and the scores from the two lists do not need to be related.
For hybrid search, pgvector suggests Postgres full-text search, merged with RRF or a
re-ranking
model.
Re-ranking adds one more step. A re-ranking model scores the top results again, and only the best ones go into the prompt. It adds some
latency
, and you trade more re-ranked chunks against speed and cost.
Chunking choices
Chunk size, chunk borders and overlap all change what retrieval finds.
A small chunk can lose its meaning. Anthropic's example is a chunk that says revenue grew by 3%, without saying which company or which quarter.
Its fix, "contextual retrieval", adds a short note about the whole document to each chunk before indexing.

Anthropic measured this on codebases, fiction, ArXiv papers and science papers. The failure rate is the share of relevant chunks missing from the top 20, averaged over these sets. Contextual embeddings plus contextual BM25 cut the top-20 retrieval failure rate by 49%, from 5.7% to 2.9%. Adding re-ranking cut it by 67%, to 1.9%.
These are their numbers on their data. Your data will differ, so measure your own.
Evaluation: measure, don't guess
Test the two halves apart.
Retrieval quality.
For each test question, write down which chunks
should
come back. Then measure
recall@k
: the share of those chunks that appear in the top k. Anthropic's study uses exactly this kind of
metric
Answer quality.
Is the answer correct, and is every claim backed by a cited chunk? Anthropic's
eval
guide says to mirror your real task mix, include edge cases, and grade automatically where you can.
If a model grades the answers, it suggests using a different model from the one that wrote them.
Our advice: start with 30 to 50 real questions from users or support tickets. Add questions where the right answer is "I don't know". Run the set after every change to
chunking
, the embedding model, top-k or the prompt.
Common failures
Wrong chunk retrieved.
The answer sounds right but cites the wrong policy. Look at the retrieved chunks first.
Stale index.
The document changed, but the old chunks are still in the index. Re-index on every change, and delete chunks of deleted documents.
Prompt injection
from documents.
A retrieved page can contain hidden instructions. OWASP calls this indirect prompt injection, and says RAG does not fully remove the risk.
Mark retrieved text clearly as untrusted data, and give the model only the access and tools it needs.
Leaking documents.
If the index holds documents for different users, weak access control can leak them. OWASP advises permission-aware vector stores.
Filter at retrieval time, not in the prompt. One trap: with approximate indexes in pgvector, a WHERE filter runs
after
the index scan, so you may get fewer results than you asked for.
Cost and latency
Each request adds steps: embed the question, search, maybe re-rank, then a longer prompt. More chunks mean more
input tokens
. Re-ranking costs time but can lower model cost, because the model reads less text.
If your whole knowledge base is under 200,000 tokens (about 500 pages), Anthropic suggests you may not need RAG at all. Put it all in the prompt and use
prompt caching
This table is our own summary, except where a source is cited.
Whole knowledge base in the prompt
Edit the text and it is live.
More tokens per call. Caching helps.
The data is small, under about 200,000 tokens.
RAG with vector search
, if you re-index on change.
Embedding and a search per question.
Users ask in their own words, and data is large.
RAG with keyword search (BM25)
Cheap and fast.
Users search for exact codes, names or IDs.
Hybrid search plus re-ranking
The most steps and the slowest.
Both kinds of question, and quality matters most.
Fine-tuning
Facts in model weights are hard to update.
The paper calls tracing facts in weights an open problem.
Our view: a training run for every change.
Our view: to change style or format, not to add facts.
Simple rule:
start with the simplest design that passes your test set. Add hybrid search or re-ranking only when the numbers show you need it.

sections.name: At work
sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: When an answer is wrong, first ask:
"Was the right chunk retrieved?"
Log the retrieved chunk IDs for every request so you can answer this.
Build the test set before you tune anything. Keep it in the repo and run it in
CI
Treat permissions as part of retrieval. Store the access rules next to each chunk, and filter in the query.
When a policy changes, re-index it the same day and add a test question for it.
Show citations in the user interface. If the model cannot cite a source, it should say it does not know.
Ask your team who owns the bot's answers. The tribunal's view was clear: the company does.
"Here are 20 real user questions and our docs folder. For each question, list the document sections that should be retrieved. Mark any question our docs cannot answer."
"Write a script that runs our RAG pipeline on this test set and prints recall@5 and the retrieved chunk IDs for each question that failed."
"Review this retrieval code. Show me every path where a chunk can reach the prompt without the user's permission check."
The expected chunks in the test set are right. Check a sample by hand, because the agent may guess.
The permission filter runs inside the search query, before the prompt is built, and a test proves it.
The test set includes questions that should get "I don't know".
Retrieved text is marked as data in the prompt, and the model has no tools it does not need.
You compared numbers before and after each change, not only a few examples.

q.v: Your support bot gives a wrong answer about the refund window. What should you check first?

options.v: Which model you use. Switch to a bigger one.
Which chunks retrieval returned for that question, and whether the right policy text was among them.

why.v: Check retrieval first. If the right text never reached the prompt, no model can answer from it.

q.v: Your index holds HR documents. Some are for managers only. Where must you enforce this?

options.v: In the prompt, by telling the model not to reveal manager-only content.
At retrieval time, so chunks the user may not read never enter the prompt.
In the user interface, by hiding the answer when it looks sensitive.

why.v: A prompt rule is advice the model may ignore. A filter at retrieval time means the model never sees what the user may not read.

q.v: Users search for error codes like "TS-999", and vector search keeps missing them. What helps most?

options.v: Add keyword search (BM25) and merge both result lists.
Ask the model to guess the error code.

why.v: Embeddings capture meaning but can miss exact strings. Keyword search finds exact terms, so hybrid search covers both.

q.v: Your whole knowledge base is about 50 pages and changes once a month. What is the simplest good design?

options.v: A vector database, a re-ranker and a chunking pipeline.
Fine-tune a model on the 50 pages.
Put all the pages in the prompt, with prompt caching.

why.v: Anthropic notes that a knowledge base under 200,000 tokens can go straight into the prompt. Our advice is to add RAG when it no longer fits.

q.v: You changed the chunk size. How do you know if it helped?

options.v: Ask three colleagues if the answers feel better.
Run your test set and compare recall@k and answer scores before and after.
Check that the build still passes.

why.v: Measure, don't guess. A fixed test set shows whether the right chunks are now found and whether answers improved.
